analysis.investment_thesis: Aadhar Housing Finance is a classic affordable-housing play with a PEG of ~0.62 (P/E 20.8 ÷ 33.4% net profit CAGR) — exactly the kind of fast grower hiding in plain sight that I love. India's underpenetrated affordable housing market, supported by PMAY tailwinds and a rising middle class, gives this company a long runway.
key_strengths: Exceptional net profit CAGR of 33.4% over 6 years (INR 162 Cr → 912 Cr), with P/E of only 20.8 — PEG of 0.62 is a textbook bargain
Revenue growing at 16.1% CAGR and accelerating (INR 2,587 Cr → 3,108 Cr in FY25), with operating income CAGR of 21.3% in last 3 years
High promoter holding (64.9%) and a simple, understandable story: lend to first-time homebuyers in Tier 2/3 India at healthy spreads
key_risks: D/E of 2.55 is inherent leverage for an HFC but leaves the balance sheet sensitive to credit cycle downturns or NPA spikes
Persistently negative operating cash flow (-3,027 Cr in FY25) — normal for a lending business but a red flag if asset quality deteriorates
Interest rate volatility squeezes net interest margins; finance costs grew from INR 799 Cr (FY23) to INR 1,174 Cr (FY25), up 47%
red_flags: NPA quality data not disclosed here — affordable housing borrowers can be more vulnerable in economic downturns
Equity base nearly doubled in FY25 (INR 4,450 Cr → 6,894 Cr), suggesting dilutive equity raise — EPS growth may lag headline profit growth
analysis.detailed_analysis: AADHARHFC checks the most important Lynch box: a fast-growing company at a price that doesn't reflect its growth. Net profits compounded at 33.4% over six years while the stock trades at just 20.8x trailing earnings — a PEG of 0.62 screams under-appreciation. The business model is straightforward: originate home loans to the first-time buyer segment (ticket sizes under INR 15 lakh) where competition from big banks is thin and demand is structurally supported by urbanisation and government housing subsidies. Operating margins have been stable-to-expanding at ~65%, and reserves have grown from INR 2,308 Cr to INR 6,461 Cr, reflecting genuine retained earnings rather than financial engineering.
